newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: PolyGram taking $90 million restructuring charge.
newsitem.headline: PolyGram taking $90 million restructuring charge.

text.p: PolyGram NV said Wednesday it would take a $90 million reorganization charge against its 1996 results, which it predicted would be flat or slightly lower because of slower than expected music sales.

The recorded music and film company, 75 percent owned by Philips Electronics NV, said the restructuring will focus on the rejuvenation of Motown, the U.S. label it acquired in 1993, and reorganization of its classical music division.

"Entering the important fourth quarter, the company currently expects the full-year 1996 operating result before restructuring charges to be flat or slightly below last year's, caused by lower than expected music sales," PolyGram said in a statement.
PolyGram said it had fallen victim to sluggish music markets worldwide but added that music sales were also lower than expected due to problems within PolyGram itself.
In 1995 PolyGram posted a net profit of 741 million guilders ($431 million), almost unchanged from 738 million in 1994.
Spokeswoman Amanda Conroy said the rejuvenation of Motown was a key goal of the planned restructuring.

"Management is taking positive steps to ... make sure that the (Motown) label rejuvenates itself with new artists," she said. "It has a fantastic back catalogue, obviously, but any record label needs to bring on new artists."
PolyGram said it was making management changes at Motown and overhauling its artist and repertoire department, which is responsible for signing new talent.
Conroy said PolyGram was also taking action to offset the effects of several years of flat sales in the market for recordings of classical music.
"The way we're addressing this problem at PolyGram is to revamp our three classical labels -- Decca, Deutsche Grammophon, Philips Classics," she said.
Conroy also said the reorganization would involve distribution and marketing operations in Europe.
